strengths: Clear unifying framework connecting DPS, global MAP, TMPD, and optimization-based inverse problem methods under a single local MAP perspective
Well-motivated objective reformulation (Eq. 13) with interpretable parameters (k₁ as trust-region, k₂ as measurement scale) and automatic annealing properties

Comprehensive experimental validation across 10 image restoration tasks and 3 scientific inverse problems with 60 total quantitative results showing consistent improvements (≥2 dB on motion deblurring, JPEG, quantization; >1.5 dB on inverse scattering)
Improved computational efficiency compared to DAPS baseline while achieving better reconstruction quality
Novel approach to handling non-differentiable operators through surrogate-gradient approximation (Sec. 4.3)
Excellent reproducibility with complete hyperparameter tables, detailed algorithms, and thorough ablation studies
Intuitive toy example (Appendix A, Figure 3) clearly illustrating distinctions between posterior mean, local MAP, and global MAP
weaknesses: Limited theoretical rigor: no convergence analysis for local MAP iterations, informal justification for why local MAP neither converges to global MAP nor equals posterior sampling, missing quantitative error analysis for Gaussian posterior approximation
Core theoretical claim (local MAP interpretation) is established somewhat circularly by parameterizing covariance as Σ₀|ₜ = λₜσ²ᵧI; this is more interpretive than revealing new insights

Unjustified design choices: isotropic covariance approximation Σ₀|ₜ ≈ k/SNR·I rests on three informal heuristics rather than rigorous justification; claim that covariance is 'nearly isotropic as t→0' is unsubstantiated
Inconsistent algorithmic treatment: for linear inverse problems with closed-form solution (Eq. 15), the algorithm uses K gradient steps anyway—motivation unclear and potentially wasteful

Extreme hyperparameter sensitivity without principled guidance: k₁ varies 0-10,000, k₂ varies 0.01-30,000, learning rates 0.005-1.0 across tasks, but paper provides no methodology for practitioners to set these on new problems

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars or significance testing on results, making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements (often 0.1-0.3 dB) are meaningful; phase retrieval comparisons use 'best of 4 runs' which biases results

Incomplete analysis of problem-dependent behavior: no explanation of why LMAPS works well on highly non-convex phase retrieval if Gaussian posterior assumption is violated, or which problem characteristics favor local MAP over DPS
Limited novelty over existing optimization methods: improvements appear to stem primarily from better objective formulation and hyperparameter choices rather than the local MAP interpretation itself

Insufficient ablation studies: no comparison of different covariance parameterizations, no independent ablation on k₁ and k₂, no ablation comparing Eq. 13 to equivalent Eq. 14 empirically, minimal exploration of surrogate choices for non-differentiable operators
Minimal discussion of recent related work (Ref. 32 on MAP estimation perspective receives only one sentence despite apparent relevance)

strengths: Clear theoretical framework distinguishing local MAP, global MAP, and DPS with effective visualizations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 13 diverse tasks (10 image restoration + 3 scientific) with extensive baseline comparisons
Strong empirical results on challenging problems with >1.5 dB gains on linear inverse scattering
Principled methodological contributions including isotropic covariance approximation and scale-invariant objective reformulation
Excellent reproducibility materials with complete hyperparameter lists, ablation studies, and theoretical proofs
Unifies optimization-based and sampling-based methods under single probabilistic framework
weaknesses: Limited novelty over concurrent DMAP work (Xu et al., 2025); clean-signal space formulation is incremental reformulation rather than fundamentally new approach
Key isotropic covariance approximation Σ₀|ₜ ≈ (k/SNR)I only theoretically justified as t→0; lacks empirical validation of when approximation breaks down and how approximation error accumulates

Extensive task-specific hyperparameter tuning (5+ parameters, Table 4) with no principled selection rule; limited ablation studies raise concerns about reproducibility and fairness of baseline comparisons

Inconsistent distributional metrics: DMAP achieves better FID on some tasks (e.g., SR: 44.78 vs 80.63), contradicting state-of-the-art claims and suggesting mode-seeking bias may hurt distributional fidelity
No convergence analysis, approximation error bounds, or rigorous analysis of mode-seeking bias implications; missing theoretical guarantees for the hybrid approach

Phase retrieval results select best of 4 runs per image, potentially inflating performance; no confidence intervals or significance tests except phase retrieval; missing comparison with DMAP on scientific tasks
